albums.blurb: Manuel Göttsching co-founded the Berlin cosmic-rock group Ash Ra Tempel before turning to solo electronic work. E2-E4 is a single hour-long piece he recorded in one take in his home studio in December 1981, layering improvised electric guitar over a two-chord sequencer pulse; it sat on the shelf until Klaus Schulze's Inteam label released it in 1984. The title comes from the standard chess opening move, and Spotify carries it as "E2-E4 (Mixed)", indexed into thirteen continuous sections.
albums.reception: Larry Levan made it a Paradise Garage staple, the 1989 Italo-house hit "Sueño Latino" was built on it, and Pitchfork and The Guardian have both named it among the best albums of the 1980s for its role in the development of house and techno.

albums.blurb: Pretzel Logic is Steely Dan's third album and the last recorded with the full original five-piece band before Walter Becker and Donald Fagen retired the group to the studio. It compresses their jazz-leaning harmony into eleven short songs, among them a faithful cover of Duke Ellington's "East St. Louis Toodle-Oo", and its session-player polish points toward the way they would work for the rest of the decade.
albums.reception: The album reached number eight on the Billboard 200, while "Rikki Don't Lose That Number" peaked at number four on the Hot 100, the biggest hit single of the band's career.

albums.blurb: Kokoroko are an eight-piece London band led by trumpeter Sheila Maurice-Grey, part of the UK jazz circle around Gilles Peterson's Brownswood label; they first drew wide attention when "Abusey Junction", their contribution to the 2018 We Out Here compilation, went viral. Could We Be More is their debut full-length, following a 2019 self-titled EP, and folds afrobeat, highlife guitar and soul harmonies into a horn-led band sound.
albums.reception: It reached number 30 on the UK Albums Chart, and Jazzwise gave it four stars as an Editor's Choice while The Guardian called it "a debut of easy-going beauty".
